title: Shortest Bridge
description: Find the minimum bridge length connecting two islands in a grid, using flood fill to identify one island and multi-source BFS to reach the other.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an n x n binary grid containing exactly two islands (maximal 4-directionally connected groups of 1s), find the minimum number of 0s that must be flipped to 1 to connect the two islands into one. Equivalently, return the minimum length of a bridge of 0-cells connecting them.

blocks.caption: A multi-source BFS from every cell of the first island finds the nearest cell of the second island.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Grid","n x n, exactly two islands, each of 4-directionally connected 1-cells"],["Move","4-directional, through 0-cells"],["Goal","Minimum number of 0-cells to flip (bridge length) to connect the two islands"],["Note","The bridge does not include the islands themselves, only the 0-cells crossed"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

The shortest distance between two connected regions in an unweighted grid is a classic multi-source BFS: treat every cell of the first island as a simultaneous starting point, and expand outward through 0-cells until any cell of the second island is reached. This is a two-step process: first identify one full island (via DFS or BFS flood fill), then BFS outward from all of its cells at once.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Multi-source BFS reuses the same layer-by-layer queue technique as single-source BFS problems like Open the Lock, just seeded with many starting points instead of one.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture two islands separated by open water. Ripples spread outward simultaneously from every point along the first island's coastline. The first moment a ripple touches the second island, the distance it traveled is exactly the shortest possible bridge length.

blocks.caption: Ripples spreading from the whole first island reach the second island at the shortest possible distance.

items: First, identify all cells of ONE island using a flood fill (DFS or BFS), marking them visited.
Seed a BFS queue with every cell of that island simultaneously, each at distance 0.
Expand through 0-cells layer by layer; the first 1-cell encountered belongs to the OTHER island, and the current layer's distance is the answer.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
grid = [[0,1,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]]. Island 1 is the single cell (0,1). BFS expands outward.

blocks.content: {"headers":["BFS layer (distance)","Cells reached"],"rows":[["0","(0,1) - island 1 itself"],["1","(1,1), (0,2), (0,0)"],["2","(2,1), (1,2), (1,0), and (2,2) which is a 1-cell, part of island 2"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The second island is first reached at distance 2 (cell (2,2)), matching the expected output. The bridge consists of 2 flipped 0-cells to connect the islands.
5. How Should We Think?
A conceptually simple but slow approach might try flipping different sets of 0-cells and checking connectivity after each, which is combinatorially infeasible.

The efficient insight: since every cell of island 1 starts a search simultaneously (distance 0), BFS naturally finds the SHORTEST path from the island's combined coastline to island 2, without needing to try individual starting cells one at a time. This is because BFS explores in strict order of increasing distance, and seeding multiple sources at once still preserves that guarantee across the whole frontier.
6. Brute Force Solution

This is already the standard efficient technique for this problem: find island 1 via DFS, then run multi-source BFS from all its cells. The "brute force" here uses recursive DFS (which can be less predictable for very large grids due to recursion depth) to find the first island before the BFS phase.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","DFS visits island 1 once, BFS visits every 0-cell at most once"],["Space","O(n^2)","Visited grid plus the BFS queue and recursion stack"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This approach is already asymptotically optimal; the risk with recursive DFS is stack depth on very large, densely connected islands (up to n^2 cells deep in the worst case).
8. Optimize the Solution

The algorithm stays the same; the main practical refinement is combining the DFS island-finding phase directly with seeding the BFS queue in one pass, avoiding a separate list allocation, and processing the BFS strictly layer by layer so the returned distance is exact without needing to store it per queue entry.

items: DFS from the first found 1-cell, marking visited and pushing each cell directly into the multi-source BFS queue.
BFS outward through unvisited 0-cells, marking each visited as it is enqueued.
The moment a 1-cell is reached during expansion, its current distance is the answer.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Multi-source BFS finds the shortest distance from ANY of several starting points simultaneously, exactly what "shortest bridge between two regions" needs.
A flood fill (DFS or BFS) is the standard way to identify one connected region before searching outward from it.
The pattern "flood fill one region, then multi-source BFS to the other" generalizes to any "shortest connection between two groups" grid problem.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Shortest Bridge is solved by first flood-filling one island to identify all its cells, then running a multi-source BFS seeded from every one of those cells simultaneously. The first 1-cell reached during this expansion belongs to the second island, and its BFS distance is exactly the minimum bridge length, all in O(n^2) time.
